title: Review: Wines of Xander Soren, 2026 Releases
summary:

The post Review: Wines of Xander Soren, 2026 Releases appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
We greatly enjoyed our last go-round with California’s Xander Soren wines, and recently the operation sent a full complement of new releases, spanning all eight of its current offerings on the market — this time including whites and reds (and one rose). Reviews are presented in order of preference.

Note that the winery’s entry-level wines are denoted by a colored label and only the name “Xander,” sans “Soren.”

2021 Xander Soren Pinot Noir Ludeon Central Coast – A supple and seductive wine, this is the pinnacle of Xander Soren’s collection and it immediately shows. Deftly balanced among notes of tart cherry, soothing raspberry, bittersweet chocolate, and orange flower blossoms, this wine weaves back and forth on the palate as it evolves in glass to coax out elements of tea leaf before finishing on a brighter touch of orange peel. Layers of walnut, darker chocolate, and hints of coffee emerge, all melding beautifully into the experience. Impossible to put down, this is American pinot at its finest. A / $195

2021 Xander Soren Pinot Noir Olivet Lane Russian River Valley – The lone RRV pinot in the mix here, I was expecting a dense monster of a wine, in keeping with the region’s typical style. Shocker: This is gentle and approachable and full of exuberance, layered with surprisingly easygoing notes of ripe cherry and strawberry, touched with tea leaf and, later, bay leaf notes. While fairly straightforward, hints of vanilla and a little chocolate force their way into a tart and fruity palate that maintains an acidic brightness from start to finish. Impossible to put down, this wine made me wholly rethink everything about pinot from the Russian River Valley. A / $125

2021 Xander Soren Pinot Noir Sanford & Benedict Sta. Rita Hills – Quite a savory expression of pinot, with a strong tomato leaf note visible up front. This sharper edge finds a complement in notes of cranberry and some extracted cherry elements, hinting at almond as the finish builds. More savory notes of tobacco leaf, bay leaf, and a touch of coffee give the conclusion a brooding character, though a final spritz of orange oil livens things up just so. Consider decanting to accelerate the development process — and pair the wine appropriately. A- / $125

2021 Xander Chardonnay Santa Barbara County – Pouring this wine — Soren’s $75 entry-level bottling — into a glass reveals an initial rush of earth and leather, but time is your friend with this one. Slowly the wine opens up as it warms to showcase evolving layers of coconut and almond nougat, with lemon curd notes offering a powerful undercurrent of tart fruit. I was initially a little put off by the hoarier elements of the experience, but thing changed with surprising speed as the lively underbelly of lemon, lime, and green apple present in the wine shifted into prominence. In short order, the wine came out of its shell and blossomed like a butterfly to reveal an exuberant muse, gently floral but still citrus-forward and palate-cleansing, a perfect pairing for a spicy dinner. A- / $75

2021 Xander Soren Chardonnay Habari Sta. Rita Hills – This single-vineyard chardonnay from the El Jabali Vineyard pours with a surprising austerity, coming across as rather bitter at the start, keeping the drinker at arm’s length as it takes its time to develop. Air and some warmth allow the wine to develop more nuance — gooseberry, pear, and some tart green apple notes all sparring with a distinctively moderated barrel character that comes off with more of an aged melon vibe. (The wine is aged in only 10% new French oak.) The level of acidity here is quite surprising, with saline notes lingering well into the finish and tempering what wood is present. Notes of honeydew inform the fade-out. Above all: Give this wine plenty of time. It’s closed off at the start, but time spent digging into it reveals far more charm than I ever expected. A- / $150

2021 Xander Soren Pinot Noir Yuki Vineyard West Sonoma Coast – Boldly cherry-forward, the expressive fruit here settles down with time to reveal earthier notes, particularly tea leaf and more muted notes of bay leaf, finishing with a chewy, tobacco-like quality. The fade-out is earthier than I expected (or desired), but when paired with a lively meal (I tried mushroom Bolognese) the combination works remarkably well. B+ / $125

2025 Xander Rose of Pinot Noir California Cuvee – I’m not sure what I was expecting with this rose, but the burst of strawberry that hits the senses immediately wasn’t it. Incredibly fruity, bordering on candylike at times, the wine is flush with fruit but also features plenty of brighter elements — lemon peel and salinity — before shifting back to feature some dried floral notes. A touch of almond informs the finish. Certainly crowd-pleasing, but not at all what I though would be in the mix. B+ / $50

2021 Xander Pinot Noir Santa Barbara County – Xander Soren’s entry-level pinot (albeit a $75 wine) strikes with a shocking smokiness, notes of underbrush aflame, dried tea leaves, and cardamom, creating a savory experience that feels more than a little blown out and aggressive. That might not be such a problem if the wine had a powerful body to stand up against the smoky onslaught, but this pinot hits the palate as distinctly thin, pale in color, with a finish that evokes weak tea — touched of course with smoke. Was wildfire an issue with this vintage in Santa Barbara? B- / $75

The post Review: Four Roses Anthology Chapter One: Origin 21 Years Old (2026) appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Jonesing for ultra-ultra-premium whiskey? Four Roses is the latest to have you covered with a unicorn offering, the first in a new luxe series called Anthology. Anthology will be an annually released whiskey, a collection of rarities designed to “explore key chapters in the brand’s 138-year history. The inaugural release, Chapter One: Origin, is a 21-year-old OBSF bourbon and the oldest release in Four Roses history.”

Taking that further: “The first chapter is inspired by Four Roses’ founding story, when founder Paul Jones Jr. named the brand after his Southern belle accepted his marriage proposal by wearing a corsage of four red roses to a grand ball in 1888. The release pays tribute to the moment that inspired the brand and the themes of love and connection that continue to define Four Roses today.”

I don’t know who’ll be able to snap up one of the 1200 bottles (mainly at the Four Roses Visitor’s Center), but, well, let’s see how it tastes.

Four Roses Anthology Chapter One: Origin 21 Years Old (2026) Review

The nose promptly showcases the age of this whiskey. Austere and tannic, the rye-forward qualities of OBSF are amplified to the hilt here, bold with cloves and extra-dark chocolate. Time in glass takes this latter note and runs with it, turning coffee-like as it develops in a Glencairn. Gravelly and intense, there’s nothing subtle about the experience, as it wholly connotes the significant density to come.

Intense and quite wine-like on the tongue, the aromatic buildup is paid off immediately. Old and layered with wood, the charry-tarry bourbon unfolds with amazing austerity, evoking tobacco leaf, leather, and tar in quick succession. If there’s fruit left in the barrel, it fully evaporates before it hits the glass: This is 100% savory, though that doesn’t mean it’s without nuance. Elements of walnut (namely shell), black pepper, burnt grass, and lingering creosote all combine to create a, well, appropriately ancient but surprisingly immersive sip. It tastes extremely old, but as a famous Monty Python character might has said, not quite dead yet. The longer it sits in the glass and on the tongue, the more its latent life is revealed. Be patient.

Ultimately, a hint of molasses on the finish gives you the lightest respite from what can be a somewhat overwhelming experience. Maybe that touch of sweetness is all it took to get me to wonder if a second taste lies somewhere in my future. Probably not, alas.

102.6 proof.

A- / $500

title: Review: Wines of Cadre, 2024 Vintage
summary:
“Cadre was built on a simple belief that California’s next great story is not Chardonnay or red wines, but fresh, aromatic white wines that reflect our coastal roots.” That’s a bold statement from a winemaker (John Niven of Cadre) who lives in a state specifically known for chardonnay and cabernet, and here he comes from…

The post Review: Wines of Cadre, 2024 Vintage appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
“Cadre was built on a simple belief that California’s next great story is not Chardonnay or red wines, but fresh, aromatic white wines that reflect our coastal roots.”

That’s a bold statement from a winemaker (John Niven of Cadre) who lives in a state specifically known for chardonnay and cabernet, and here he comes from the San Luis Obispo Coast with an armload of… albarino and gruner veltliner? Ballsy.

Cadre recently sent us a four pack of its recent releases, which we put through their paces. Thoughts follow.

2024 Cadre Sea Queen Albarino – Tropical and vibrant, this fruit-forward wine packs in a pinch of salinity to add a lively mineral character to what otherwise hits with bright pineapple and crisp lemon notes. That steely acidity prevents the wine from blowing out the way your typical pinot grigio can do, leading to a balanced finish that finds room for touches of coconut and lychee. Beautiful. A

2024 Cadre Stone Blossom Sauvignon Blanc – This is a boldly tropical — and surprisingly peachy — expression of sauvignon blanc, sweeter and creamier than most expressions, though it’s quite a delight thanks to its fruity exuberance, culminating in a surprisingly vanilla-heavy finish. A latent punch of green apple ensures the wine stays on target for the varietal and never becomes overly unctuous and sugary, though I have to confess the mix of fresh fruit and sweeter elements make this a wholly iconic porch pounder — in the best possible way. A-

2024 Cadre Beautiful Stranger – A blend of 60% gruner veltliner, 30% sauvignon blanc, 10% albarino. This is a surprising blend that I didn’t expect would work as well as it does, the boldly tropical notes of the sauvignon blanc (and albarino) complemented by the tart acidity of the gruner. Together they make for a cohesive and expressive wine that perks up right away with lemon, lime, and gentle tropical notes, then slowly reveals light-handed touches of marzipan and vanilla cream. While the attack feels deft, the ultimately chewy, rounded body serves to amplify all of the above. A-

2024 Cadre Band of Stones Gruner Veltliner – This doesn’t come across, much at all, like a typical gruner, with a muddy-doughy body that evoked mushroom more than the bright citrus and herbal notes you normally find with the grape. It’s a curious whiff given how delightful and acidic the Beautiful Stranger (60% gruner) tends to be, though it’s fortunate that things open up a bit after the wine gets some air on it. Settle in for the long run and you should find this becoming increasingly approachable. B

each $30

title: Review: Aviation Cranberry & Blood Orange Gin
summary:
Venerable Aviation Gin — now celebrating 20 years in existence — recently dropped a new expression, part of a small but growing collection of gins that are brightly hued instead of transparent. And while it’s a dark red color, don’t call it sloe gin. This is Aviation, infused with cranberry and blood orange elements. Now…

The post Review: Aviation Cranberry & Blood Orange Gin appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Venerable Aviation Gin — now celebrating 20 years in existence — recently dropped a new expression, part of a small but growing collection of gins that are brightly hued instead of transparent. And while it’s a dark red color, don’t call it sloe gin. This is Aviation, infused with cranberry and blood orange elements. Now owned by Diageo, it’s the first ever “flavor innovation” from the brand.

The concept is fairly self-explanatory, taking standard Aviation Gin and infusing it with cranberry and blood orange flavors — and colors, though they aren’t all natural. Certified and caramel colors are both noted on the bottle.

With that all set up, let’s dive in.

Aviation Cranberry & Blood Orange Gin Review

Visually this gin immediately connotes “cosmopolitan,” and that’s not an accident. It looks, smells, and tastes like a cosmo — just run through the gin still for a little extra sabor. The nose features both fruit components in spades — perhaps leaning more heavily into the blood orange than the cranberry, which is a bit of a surprise. Traditional gin elements are more fleeting. Juniper is indistinct to the point of ephemera, earthier notes like angelica are absent altogether. If anything, there’s just a hint of lemon peel in the mix, but this may well just be an afterimage of the powerful blood orange component.

The palate is sweet and tart; there’s definitely some sugar in the mix here, and the cosmopolitan character continues — even more so, thanks to the sweetness. Tart cranberry and blood orange peel are well-complemented by the sweetness, which comes across with a honey-like character as it lingers on the tongue. Late-game touches of milk chocolate and vanilla only amplify the cocktail qualities of the gin, which again fails to exhibit much in the way of herbal tradition save for perhaps a touch of mint.

Shaken and served in a martini glass, your guests may well be unable to tell the difference between this and a $15 cosmo at their favorite sassy watering hole — though the abv will likely bruise them a bit. Consider a splash of soda, or, better yet, serving this as part of a long drink with soda or tonic.

80 proof.

A- / $28

title: Review: NV Ferreira Porto Dona Antonia Reserva Tawny
summary:

Edged with traditional raisin notes, the Port surprises by showcasing some notable strawberry and blueberry elements, fading from there into milk chocolate and, eventually, a tea leaf character…

The post Review: NV Ferreira Porto Dona Antonia Reserva Tawny appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
While Tawny Port is known for its nutty, caramelized flavors, this expression from Ferreira’s Dona Antonia label defies expectations, perhaps owing to a relatively brief aging cycle.

Edged with traditional raisin notes, the Port surprises by showcasing some notable strawberry and blueberry elements, fading from there into milk chocolate and, eventually, a tea leaf character that fits more closely with the Tawny style. Things turn quite sweet and syrupy as the finish builds, evoking caramel and molasses flavors that had me thinking about Milk Duds candies. Vanilla lingers on the soothing conclusion — again, very sweet.

While not quite what I was expecting, it’s still a lively Port, especially at this price. I’d pair it with blue cheese to help counterbalance some of the sweeter notes.

B+ / $22

title: Review: Blue Run Blueprint Series (2026)
summary:
Next up from Blue Run is the first release in a new series of bourbons called the Blue Run Blueprint Series, which the distillery describes as “a series that celebrates the nuance found by pushing boundaries into uncharted territories – this inaugural release serves as the blueprint for what is to come.” Blueprint Series #1…

The post Review: Blue Run Blueprint Series (2026) appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Next up from Blue Run is the first release in a new series of bourbons called the Blue Run Blueprint Series, which the distillery describes as “a series that celebrates the nuance found by pushing boundaries into uncharted territories – this inaugural release serves as the blueprint for what is to come.”

Blueprint Series #1 is a blend of two unique mashbills: one wheated, the other “an experimental mash that pays homage to Blue Run’s boundary-pushing nature.” That experimental mash is — wait for it — an 80% corn, 15% rye, 5% malted barley mash that was aged on a lower floor of Blue Run’s rickhouse — a contrast to the wheated mashbill stock that was aged on a top floor. And yes, I’ll agree that a 15% rye bourbon does not exactly sound “experimental,” but let’s give Blue Run the benefit of the doubt for the moment.

“When crafting Blue Run releases, I think about the qualities bourbon enthusiasts expect, while also considering how we invite new consumers into the category,” said Shaylyn Gammon, Blue Run Spirits’ Head of Whiskey and Innovation. “With the Blueprint Series, the goal was to create a Kentucky Straight Bourbon Whiskey that can serve as a blueprint for discovery—something approachable and soft, yet layered enough to inspire continued exploration.”

Got it? Let’s give it a spin.

Blue Run Blueprint Series Kentucky Straight Bourbon Whiskey Review

If Blue Run’s goal was to create a base whiskey — a blueprint, sure — upon which to innovate, then they’ve done an admirable job. This is an approachable but reasonably complex whiskey that gives enthusiasts plenty to think about while offering a little something for everybody.

Things kick off on a nose that evokes banana cream, vanilla custard, and a surprising complement of potpourri, taking the focus off of fruit and sugar and onto the garden. The aromatics move back and forth between these two realms, punctuated by a boozy sharpness that’s driven by a 52.5% abv. The whiskey can handle plenty of water (and it mixes well), so don’t be shy.

The palate is more straightforward, though its caramel-banana core is naturally interrupted by the florals on the nose — particularly if you leave your (actual) nose stuck in the glass. Things take a turn toward chocolate as the whiskey sits on the palate for a bit, with touches of mint and an apple butter character coming into view as the finish builds. The finish is surprisingly juicy and bursting with berry notes — the latter most evident with a touch of water added.

At $70, this feels like a solid price for a solid whiskey, one which has a bigger story to tell than you might expect at first blush.

105 proof.

A- / $70

title: Bar Review: La Petite Grocery, New Orleans
summary:
More of a neighborhood bistro than a bar, La Petite Grocery has been a fixture in the Uptown district since 2004 — and under its current management since 2010. Chef Justin Devillier won a James Beard Award in 2016 for his upscale New Orleans fare, and having spent an evening here during the recent Tales…

The post Bar Review: La Petite Grocery, New Orleans appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
More of a neighborhood bistro than a bar, La Petite Grocery has been a fixture in the Uptown district since 2004 — and under its current management since 2010. Chef Justin Devillier won a James Beard Award in 2016 for his upscale New Orleans fare, and having spent an evening here during the recent Tales of the Cocktail conference, it’s easy to see why. Massive plates of Cajun delights filled our table — alongside gentle spins on classic cocktails, too.

I’m going to break tradition and talk about the food first, with which I was unable to find much fault. The blue crab beignets are a signature dish here, and the two-bite delights rightfully earn their place as one of NOLA’s most essential single dishes. A short rib appetizer bursts with beefy flavor, and a simply prepared redfish dish felt straight off the boat. As we were dining on a Monday, red beans and rice were on the menu, a massive plate served with cornbread and topped with a showstopping chicken thigh that I couldn’t put down. If you come hungry — and you’ll need to — spending an extra seven bucks on the biggest bowl of French fries in town is the best move you can make.

Of course, we’re here for the drinks, and they didn’t disappoint. We tried four items on the curated cocktail list (all $13 to $18), all classics made with something of a twist.

My favorite was a surprise called the Cassius Club, made with Tito’s vodka, apricot, Steen’s syrup, lemon, and absinthe. I almost never drink vodka cocktails but this refreshing and summery libation was perfect on a blazing hot New Orleans day. The apricot pops without being overwhelming, while the lemon and licorice-laced absinthe make for a seductive finish.

The most unique cocktail in the lineup that I tried was the Bittersweet Motel, a mix of Novo Fogo cachaca, Tempus Fugit banana liqueur, Fernet Paesani, and Bitterman’s Xocolatl Mole Bitters. It sounds wild and it is, and while our server described it as a (loose) riff on a Negroni, it took some mental gymnastics to make that connection. I especially enjoyed this as the ice melted a bit, coaxing the banana flavor from the middle ground to a dominant position on the palate.

More traditional fare included tastes of a Bee’s Knees (Bombay gin, honey, lavender, and lemon), with understated spice and smoldering honey, and the Blood Oath, a pumped-up version of a Blood and Sand, made with Michter’s rye, Cherry Heering, falernum, orange, and lime. It was the only cocktail in the bunch that I felt might be a bit too over the top, its fruit notes becoming overwhelming in the end.

Service here was gracious and extremely friendly, our server taking time to chat through the history of the establishment and a bit of her own journey — all managing to avoid feeling like we were being schooled while sitting in a classroom. I’ll definitely be back.

4238 Magazine St, New Orleans, LA 70115
lapetitegrocery.com

title: Review: Mount Gay Exceptionally Aged 15 Years Old and 25 Years Old
summary:
Barbados’ Mount Gay surprised us recently with the launch of a new rum collection: Exceptionally Aged. As you can imagine, the focus of these releases will be extended maturation, with the first two offerings hitting 15 and 25 years of age, respectively. Both are aged entirely in ex-bourbon casks at the distillery in Barbados and…

The post Review: Mount Gay Exceptionally Aged 15 Years Old and 25 Years Old appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Barbados’ Mount Gay surprised us recently with the launch of a new rum collection: Exceptionally Aged. As you can imagine, the focus of these releases will be extended maturation, with the first two offerings hitting 15 and 25 years of age, respectively. Both are aged entirely in ex-bourbon casks at the distillery in Barbados and include no added sugar or flavoring. Three generations of Mount Gay Master Blenders — Jerry Edwards, Allen Smith, and current Master Blender Trudiann Branker — collaborated on these initial releases.

Mount Gay Exceptionally Aged 15 Years Old Review

Even at 15 years of age (all in ex-bourbon casks), this rum hits the nose with exuberant freshness, filled with apple-driven fruit and fully laced with caramel and vanilla. Brown butter notes are insistent and arrive alongside a healthy baking spice complement. There’s so much of it on the nose that this could easily be used as a spiced rum for mixing, assuming your pockets have a bit of extra coin in them.

Things are a bit more austere on the palate, which settles into a slightly winey groove that’s backed up by ample barrel char and overtones of cocoa powder and ground coffee, the spice hitting a bit more savory, with a cardamom quality and a pinch of saffron. An initial rush of sweetness tempers as the finish leans into notes of toasted coconut, grapefruit peel, and red wine. Refined and, in the end, rather mysterious. 4942 bottles produced.

86 proof. A- / $90

Mount Gay Exceptionally Aged 25 Years Old Review

At 25 years of age, things really start to get wild. The nose is shockingly dry — and quite winey, evoking thoughts of sherry even though this rum has no wine cask involvement at all. Austere with overtones of furniture polish and leather, the rum’s aromatic profile soon turns rather ashy, with creosote notes becoming dominant in time.

The palate perks up quickly with notes of coconut, orange, and a light honey character, but this all evaporates almost immediately. Notes of very dark chocolate replace all of the above, leading to a finish that is dry as dust, though some tight notes of toasted coconut and bitter orange peel linger. Has this rum simply sat in the Caribbean heat for too long, burning away all its charm? Those in a better headspace than me may enjoy it, but I really can’t see it any other way except to call this one simply too far gone for easy consumption. 2376 bottles produced.

92 proof. B / $199

title: Review: 2022 Aesthetic Cabernet Sauvignon California
summary:
A “California” designation on a bottle of cabernet sauvignon is usually a kiss of budgety death, but this wine combats expectations from the jump. Aesthetic’s 2022 cab is easily mistakeable for a midrange Napa release, juicy with plums and currants en route to notes of baking spice, dusted with orange peel and touched lightly with…

The post Review: 2022 Aesthetic Cabernet Sauvignon California appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
A “California” designation on a bottle of cabernet sauvignon is usually a kiss of budgety death, but this wine combats expectations from the jump.

Aesthetic’s 2022 cab is easily mistakeable for a midrange Napa release, juicy with plums and currants en route to notes of baking spice, dusted with orange peel and touched lightly with oak. A hint of bay leaf gives the finish a slightly savory bent, though the sweetness of the currant notes wavers only slightly. The finish evokes chocolate sauce, Hershey’s, with a sharp touch of cherry.

A very solid choice for the price.

A- / $40

title: Review: Green River Distillery Select Toasted Double Oak Bourbon
summary:
Bardstown Bourbon Co. has had no shortage of success with their newish Distillery Reserve Series, a collection of consistently impressive and unique whiskeys available exclusively to distillery visitors and members of their whiskey club, The Reserve. Now, their sister distillery in Owensboro, Green River, is getting in on the action with its own exclusive series…

The post Review: Green River Distillery Select Toasted Double Oak Bourbon appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Bardstown Bourbon Co. has had no shortage of success with their newish Distillery Reserve Series, a collection of consistently impressive and unique whiskeys available exclusively to distillery visitors and members of their whiskey club, The Reserve. Now, their sister distillery in Owensboro, Green River, is getting in on the action with its own exclusive series dubbed Distillery Select.

While Bardstown’s Distillery Reserve Series tends to focus on exotic finishes and blends containing double digit age statement whiskeys, the new Distillery Select Series will reportedly “celebrate straightforward innovations,” meaning more traditional offerings with more modest age statements that will showcase different proofs, classic finishes, and specific rickhouse selections. The price point is also more accessible, coming in at half the cost of Bardstown’s offerings.

That’s not to say these aren’t special whiskeys, as is clear with this debut release. To kick things off, Green River is bottling their oldest bourbon to date, an eight-year-old made from their flagship mashbill of 70% corn, 21% rye, and 9% malted barley. Just thirteen barrels were chosen for the release, each finished for six months in a light char, medium toast new American oak barrel coopered by Independent Stave Company. Thoughts follow.

Green River Distillery Select Toasted Double Oak Bourbon Review

The nose is a bit soft at first, but given time to bloom, it delivers a rich bouquet that’s impressively dynamic. Early notes of Demerara sugar and cocoa powder are light and airy yet suggestive of the darker, richer sweetness to come. Undertones of baked apples and caramelized peach cobbler arrive in short order, adding a fruity depth. As things bloom even further, the fruit gives way to light roast coffee bean, maple candies, and sweet sawdust, all laced with cinnamon syrup. It’s a pleasure just to nose.

On the palate, things are well-spiced right out of the gate with bold notes of black pepper, burnt sugar, clove syrup, and tart black cherry that simmer with a hugging, chili pepper warmth across the sip. The flavors are wood driven to be sure, but they never come across astringent or over-oaked. In fact, this is one of the more balanced double oak expressions I’ve tasted. What few tannins present initially soften completely into the midpalate amid additional notes of Belgian chocolate, dark caramel, split vanilla bean, and a slightly smoky hint of charred marshmallow. The finish is rich and silky, with warm notes of baking spice and chocolate-covered caramels.

This debut Distillery Select release from Green River almost rivals some of the pricier and more exotic distillery-only whiskeys from Bardstown. There’s no club (yet) for these rare whiskeys, so you’ll have to get to Owensboro or Green River’s tasting room in Louisville to sample for yourself.

115.1 proof.

A- / $50
